title: Origin of the tune You Don't Love Me and the True lawsuit
summary: He traces the tune from Celestin's and Ridgley's bands to Don Albert and Paul Gayten and the royalties dispute.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I made Duke Ellington's Ringin' Bells. Oh yeah, I remember that. And I put that on. And I'll tell you about those recordings. Then I was the first one made this number, You Don't Love Me. You see the right name wasn't You Don't Love Me. That's the name of Paul Gaithin made it and called it True.

Yeah, it's the same thing. You see that was a tune, I think it was Feynman's son was going up to Tulane. And it was his number. And he told Celestad's band that he had this number and anything they could do with it, you know, they could have it. And so John Porter, the bass player, he was hunting and he wrote the lead of it down. And saying he gave them the words. And they began to play it because Celestad and Ridgely band was, they were together then. Yeah. And so finally he wrote it, they wrote it down and they began to play it. And then everybody began to like it, like this, this number. So Ridgely and Celestad's band split up. So Ridgely hired Don Albert and Contrell to work with him. So they worked with him and they learned, they learned the tune. And so after they find out it was Domain, well when they went to Texas, Don Albert used it for his theme song and they wrote it and I made the recording of it and they asked me, was it my tune? And I told them, I said, well no it don't belong to me. You know, in fact, at that time I just know that Celestad and I was playing it. See, and I didn't know who it belonged to either. I said, well it's just a tune they play around now. I said, I don't know who it belonged. So I could have claimed it then. So Don Albert recorded after me. He recorded the same tune with his big band. And that's where they copyrighted and they called it, you know, he said it was him and Contrell. So Paul Gaeton played with Don Albert about a month and he learned the tune and then he thought the name of it was True. You see, it's the You Don't Love Me. So when he thought about it, he recorded it and he named it, he called it True. And that's where the thing got to be, it made quite a hit with Paul Gaeton doing. But it seemed like they had some kind of lawsuit over the royalties. I mean, it looked like the company didn't want to give a, yeah.
Yeah, they didn't know who to pay it to I guess.
Yeah, well they didn't know who to pay it to because they had the copyright.

Yeah, and Paul didn't try to collect the royalties. He didn't try to collect the royalties as a writer. But it seemed like they had some trouble, Don and Contrell. And Contrell, I think they said they got something and somebody said they didn't, so I don't know. Yeah. But I thought I wouldn't say.
